title: Database Replication
intro: One database is a single point of failure and a read bottleneck. Replication keeps copies of your data on several machines.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.subtitle: Copies of the same data.
slides.explain: Replication continuously copies data from one database server to others. If one machine fails, another still has the data, and reads can be spread across the copies.

slides.heading: Primary-replica
slides.subtitle: One writer, many readers.
slides.explain: All writes go to the primary. Replicas copy its changes and serve reads. Most apps read far more than they write, so this scales well.

slides.heading: Replication lag
slides.subtitle: Replicas can be slightly behind.
slides.explain: With asynchronous replication, a replica can lag behind the primary. A user who just edited their profile might briefly see the old version if the read hits a replica.
points: Read your own writes from the primary

slides.heading: Failover
slides.subtitle: When the primary dies.
slides.explain: If the primary fails, a replica is promoted to become the new primary. Managed databases can do this automatically.
points: A replica becomes the new primary
Async setups can lose the latest writes

slides.heading: When to use it
slides.subtitle: Signs you need replicas.
slides.explain: Replication is usually the next step after caching when the database becomes the bottleneck.

scenario.situation: A social app's single database handles everything, and feed loads are most of the traffic.
scenario.problem: Read traffic saturates the database, so writes like new posts become slow too.
scenario.fix: Add two read replicas and send feed reads to them. The primary now handles mostly writes, and both get faster.
scenario.takeaway: Replicas scale reads; the primary handles writes.
